summary:
Selangor stands under Malaysia's national framework, which criminalises gender nonconformity and same-sex conduct at two separate levels. At federal level, sections 377A to 377D of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records that these provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, and are usable against transgender people. They are not limited to Malaysian citizens and reach foreign visitors.

At state level, every one of Malaysia's 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences reach Muslims only and are enforced by state Islamic religious departments, which are given wide discretion because the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer in Selangor without loosening the federal one. In 2021 the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding the state's legislative power. The federal Penal Code offences remain fully intact, and the High Court separately denied a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, filed after the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Selangor's religious authorities have pursued gender nonconformity with unusual intensity. In 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in a Selangor court to answer charges of "insulting Islam" based on her attire. The state religious department issued an arrest warrant and announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand; she was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister stated that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out enforcement actions against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked.

Criminal process against individuals continues alongside the hunt-and-warrant pattern. A Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. By June 2021 at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes", part of a crackdown on the LGBT community under way since the 2018 election; Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters found these programmes internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred. Their investigations covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, showing that Selangor sits inside a multi-state enforcement pattern rather than standing apart from it.

Queue-and-venue raids create the sharpest exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022; media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, and 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang, Selangor on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats have drawn substantial attendance, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
Selangor's legal exposure is best read against the national pattern rather than in isolation. All 13 states plus the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya carry equivalent cross-dressing offences, and the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters investigations spanned seven jurisdictions including Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, indicating a coordinated enforcement culture rather than isolated state zeal.

The Federal Court rulings point in opposite directions on the two layers of law. Selangor's Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 provisions fell in 2021 on federalism grounds, and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions fell in February 2024 on the same reasoning, while sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code were left untouched. Litigation has therefore redistributed risk between layers without reducing the total.

Foreign visitors have featured in the recent raid record. More than 130 people were held at one point after the 28 November 2025 Chow Kit sauna operation, among them 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened, which indicates consular exposure is a live possibility in venue-based arrests.

The Nur Sajat case shows how far authorities will go to enforce rigid gender norms: 122 religious-affairs officers were mobilised, an extradition request followed her flight to Thailand, and she ultimately resettled in Australia after UNHCR protection. International bodies have intervened directly, with the International Commission of Jurists demanding revocation of Jawi's enforcement licence.

Political conditions constrain any expectation of legislative relief. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, and LGBT events and media content are censored, so the framework a visitor enters is not expected to soften in the near term.
localsOnly:
Residents who are Muslim remain exposed to the state Sharia layer that foreign non-Muslim visitors are not. Cross-dressing and "a man posing as a woman" offences carry up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and enforcement sits with the state Islamic religious department, which operates without a legal definition of the conduct it polices.

Selangor residents have been processed through criminal court for gender presentation and same-sex conduct. A Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane, and state authorities issued an arrest warrant against a trans businesswoman who failed to appear before court over charges of "insulting Islam".

State "rehabilitation" programmes function as an administrative sanction. At least 1,733 people had attended them by June 2021 under the post-2018 crackdown, and documented accounts describe the programmes as internalising discrimination and fomenting self-hatred among participants.

Residents also bear exposure under the federal Penal Code, which applies regardless of gender, consent or citizenship, and which was used to charge 208 men in the Chow Kit sauna raid of 28 November 2025. Identity leaks in that operation reached the public record, with detainees' faces and personal details published and 17 civil servants suspended.

Physical safety is not secured by the litigation record. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third such killing in under two months, and the documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

There is no same-sex marriage, no anti-discrimination statute and no legal recognition of gender identity to rely on for protection, and there is no anti-discrimination law covering employment, housing or services.
outOfScopeNotes:
Two unresolved points sit around the 2021 Federal Court ruling on the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995. The sources state that provisions were struck down as exceeding state power, but do not specify which sections fell or whether the state has enacted replacement provisions; the scope of what remains enforceable in Selangor is therefore not sourced here.

The status of the constitutional challenge filed after the mass arrest of 16 trans women on 8 June 2014 is unresolved. The sources record that a challenge was pending as of late 2014 but give no later outcome.

No Selangor-specific raid data is sourced. The venue-raid record cited here comes from Kuala Lumpur and Penang operations, and whether equivalent operations have been conducted within Selangor's boundaries is not established by this inventory.

The sources do not state the current sentence tariff actually imposed under sections 377A to 377D in reported cases, only the statutory maximum of twenty years plus whipping.

Whether the Home Minister's December 2025 suggestion of revisiting the provisions produced any legislative or prosecutorial change is unresolved; the inventory records only that the proposal was floated days after the Chow Kit raid.

Emigration and re-entry consequences for transgender visitors whose passports do not match their presentation are not covered by these sources.
